title: Riding the ox home
hookLine: sixth picture: he rides the ox home, playing the flute
carry: practice turned to ease, still heading home

lines: EVENING, A PATH THROUGH THE FIELDS.
cards: Evening. A path through the fields. An ox walks slowly toward a village, and on its back sits a man who isn't holding the rope at all.
He has a flute to his lips, playing a simple tune, the kind children sing. Sometimes he looks up at the clouds. The ox knows the way.
Two pictures ago this same animal was dragging him toward the hills. In the sixth oxherding picture, there's nothing left to hold.

teach.b: First, the struggle is over. The preface says it plainly, in paraphrase: the struggle has ended, and gain and loss no longer grip him. The rope that went taut in the fourth picture has nothing left to do.
What was effort has become ease.
Second, the flute. He plays country songs, the preface says, the tunes of woodcutters and children. Nothing grand, nothing that needs an audience.
In this teaching, practice that's gone deep doesn't look solemn. It looks relaxed, even a little playful.
Third, he doesn't turn back. If someone calls to him, the preface says, he won't look back; if someone tugs at him, he won't stop. Ease isn't drifting.
He's going home, and he isn't distracted from it. Fourth, home. Some Zen teachers read home as one's own original nature, the place the search set out from.
He isn't traveling somewhere new; he's going back. His eyes are on the sky, because the path no longer needs watching.
On an ordinary day, riding home can look like a practice you no longer have to force: a walk you take because you like it, a pause before meals that just happens.
The verse ends, in paraphrase, by saying that whoever knows this melody needs no words.

how: Zen teachers use the sixth oxherding picture to describe a stage where practice no longer feels like a fight, and the image of the herdsman playing the flute on the ox's back also appears in Zen painting.

o: ease after struggle: the way home with nothing left to hold
leaving practice behind once the hard part is done
racing back to town before the ox breaks free again

p: country songs, the tunes of children
read by some as one's original nature

s: in the sixth picture the herdsman is still pulling hard on the rope
the struggle is over; he rides at ease and plays the flute.
the preface says he won't turn back if someone calls him
ease isn't drifting; he keeps going home.
the picture shows deep practice as grim and solemn
its sign of a settled mind is a man playing simple songs on the way home.

games.q: you're riding the ox home, flute in hand. someone on the roadside calls your name and tugs your sleeve. what does the sixth picture say?
o: you don't turn back; you keep riding home.
you grab the rope tight in case the ox bolts.
games.why: the preface says that if called, he won't turn, and if pulled, he won't stop. the ease of the picture comes with a clear direction.

practice: Sit however feels comfortable, and let the breath do what it's already doing, without steering it. If a sound arrives, let it be music; if a thought calls, you don't have to turn around.
The ox knows the way, so fix nothing, and if a small smile shows up, let it stay.

wordCard.voice: Riding home. The sixth oxherding picture: the struggle over, the herdsman rides the ox home playing a flute, untroubled by gain and loss. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (qiniu guijia): 'riding the ox, returning home', the name of the sixth oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: practice turned to ease, still heading home. No hand on the rope, and nowhere else to be. Enjoy the ride.
